source: Qiao, Gilday, Xie, Hughes (2025) Lang2Morph: Language-Driven Morphological Design of Robotic Hands
finding: Closest found LLM pipeline to 'build a design space, filter by hard constraints, vary by cues': LLM writes a symbolic hand grammar and parameters, code filters by 6 hard rules (finger count, link size, slenderness, length, angle, print volume), and variant-specific cues force different layouts.
numbers: 90 morphologies (3 grasp types x 10 tasks x 3 variants). Morphology Validity Rate: random 0.16; zero-shot ChatGPT 0.52, Gemini 0.28, Llama-3.1 0.17, Qwen-2.5 0.18; Lang2Morph ChatGPT 0.82, Gemini 0.79, Llama 0.53, Qwen 0.69. Diversity score 0.64 (sd 0.13) with cues vs 0.27 (sd 0.07) with cues removed.
quote: In this ablated setting, the average score drops substantially to 0.27
limits: Robot hands, not a Zwicky box. Small N, no human judges, no equal-token comparison, diversity metric is the authors' own mix of text, graph and geometry. Validity is rule-based, not real-world tested.
agent_relevance: Supports the split: LLM proposes, code checks hard rules, cues force variety. For the same model, validity went from 0.52 to 0.82 with the pipeline; diversity cues more than doubled the diversity score.

source: Yun, Peng, Shang (2025) UltraGen: Extremely Fine-grained Controllable Generation
finding: When one generation must satisfy many attribute constraints at once, LLM constraint satisfaction falls as attribute count grows; later attributes in the prompt are dropped more. Fine-tuning (not scaffolding) gives only 5-10 point gains.
numbers: At 50 simultaneous attributes (Llama-3.2-3B): constraint satisfaction rate base 37.40%, auto-reconstruction 35.86%, plus global preference optimisation 44.76%. Typical benchmarks use 3-5 constraints; degradation reported by 30+ (also GPT-4o, Fig 1). LLM judge agreement with human check 84.55%.
limits: Small model; training based; CSR judged by an LLM. Not a morphological study.
agent_relevance: Boundary for a wide box: filling a cell with 10+ parameter values in one pass will lose some values. Have code assemble the cell, and verify each value after generation (G) instead of trusting one long prompt.

source: Feng, Wang, Cheng, Wan, Chen (2025) Are We on the Right Way to Assessing LLM-as-a-Judge? (Sage)
finding: Tests pairwise-judge self-consistency without human labels. Judges flip when pair order is reversed and break transitivity, more so when options are close in quality. Self-written rubrics reduce it.
numbers: 650 questions, 13 LLMs. Overall intra-pair instability (IPI) on easy set: Gemini-2.5-Pro 0.072, GPT-5-Chat 0.143, Claude-3-Haiku 0.279. Hard set: Gemini-2.5-Pro 0.250, GPT-5-Chat 0.436. Top models inconsistent in nearly a quarter of hard cases; about 200% more inconsistency when options are close; self-generated rubrics cut IPI by 16.1% and TOV by 11.0%; panels up to 15% better.
limits: This measures consistency, not accuracy against domain experts, and uses answer quality, not 'are values A and B compatible'. No morphological data.
agent_relevance: Closest numbers for gap 3: a pairwise judge flips on swapped order in about 7-28% of pairs (easy) and 25-44% (hard). Ask each compatibility pair in both orders or with a rubric and vote; treat disagreement as unknown and pass it to verification.

source: Terwiesch, Meincke, Girotra, Mollick, Nave, Ulrich (2026) AI and Its Impact on Creativity and Diversity: LLM-Generated Product Ideas (Study 3b)
finding: Direct test of forcing variety by injecting random constraints, personas or sonnets, versus chain of thought and independent sessions. Random functional constraints (close to filling a random cell of an attribute box) beat plain sampling; independent one-idea sessions and 'make it bolder' refinement hurt diversity.
numbers: Diversity = 1 minus mean pairwise cosine similarity, 100 ideas per condition, GPT-4o: humans 0.773; random personas 0.757; human-picked problem + AI solution 0.739; random functional constraints 0.735; chain of thought 0.698; random sonnets 0.686; plain 0.679; bold-refinement x2 0.575; independent sessions 0.452.
limits: One task (student products under $50), embedding cosine as diversity, quality not matched across arms. 'Constraints' are single random requirements, not full combination boxes. Eccentric prompts did not give monotone gains.
agent_relevance: Evidence that random-constraint injection (a degenerate box) lifts diversity by 0.056 over plain; supports sampling cells by code. Warns that serial refine-the-best loops converge and that fully independent sampling is not automatically diverse.

source: Terwiesch et al. (2026) same paper, Study 3a: models, temperature and pooling
finding: Newer models are more diverse, but no single model reaches human diversity; pooling ideas across four vendors reaches about human level. Cross-run homogeneity is largely a model property.
numbers: Diversity: humans 0.773; composite pool of 4 vendors 0.763 (not different from humans, p=.092); GPT-4 Turbo 0.756; Gemini 2.0 Pro 0.752; DeepSeek R1 0.752; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.682; GPT-4o 0.679; GPT-4 (2023) 0.585; o3-mini 0.495 (fixated on desk organisers). GPT-4o at temperature 0 gives 0.618 vs 0.679 at 1.0.
limits: 2000 ideas per model, 100 drawn. One product task. Release-date trend not monotone.
agent_relevance: For gap 8: homogeneity is a cross-model and cross-run problem; a box alone cannot be assumed to fix it. Combine box cells with varied personas and track pairwise similarity across runs.

source: Terwiesch et al. (2026) same paper, Study 3c: scaling the number of ideas
finding: Brute generation volume closes the coverage gap to human ideas slowly and not fully.
numbers: Mean nearest-neighbour cosine distance from 200 human ideas to the closest LLM idea: 0.546 at N=100 to 0.478 at N=1,000, no plateau. Maximum distance (hardest human idea) only 0.762 to 0.711.
limits: Coverage is measured relative to human ideas, not all feasible ideas.
agent_relevance: A free-sampling baseline for gaps 1 and 6: ten times the tokens moved mean coverage distance by 0.068. A box test must beat that at equal tokens.

source: Yearsley and Kurteva (2026) Investigating Stability and Consensus in LLM Taxonomy Generation (SEMANTiCS 2026 poster, CEUR Vol-4293)
finding: An LLM groups 41 puzzle games into a taxonomy, repeatedly. Coverage is near perfect, but the grouping differs from run to run; a consensus core can be extracted from repeats.
numbers: 9 models, 3 providers, 324 runs. Mean F1 0.995, hallucinated names 0.068 per run. Share of sibling pairs that are siblings in every run: 0.285 overall; T=0 0.391 vs T=1 0.178; prompt Basic 0.231, specify-example 0.249, specify-example-categories 0.374; with rules PDF 0.328 vs 0.241 without. Consensus core at 0.5 threshold: 40 pairs, 28 games.
quote: a single LLM run cannot be treated as a reliable classification
limits: Poster-length, one domain, entities supplied, not dimension choice for design. Richest taxonomies were not the most stable ones.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 4 by proxy: grouping and category choice is unstable run to run (about 0.18-0.39 of pairs repeat). Run box-building several times, keep recurring dimensions as the core, list the rest as extras, and use low temperature.

source: Nakashima, Ishimoto, Kondo, Xiao, Kamei (2026) How Well Do LLMs Generate Taxonomies in the SE Domain?
finding: Five-run protocol on taxonomy generation: staged pipelines (TnT-LLM, CLIMB) differ in stability; judge noise is small compared with generation noise. Only the first pages and tables were read.
numbers: Pipelines compared on 12 quality criteria across generators (GPT-5.2, Gemini-3-Pro, DeepSeek-V3.2, Llama 4 Maverick, Mistral Large 3). TnT-LLM near human quality; CLIMB lower on non-overlap (mean difference 0.313, p<0.05) and structure (CEDS 0.461, p<0.001). Range across 5 repeats smaller for CLIMB.
limits: Partly read; taxonomies of software artefacts, not design parameters.
agent_relevance: Second independent hint for gap 4: the structure of an LLM-built category set varies by run and pipeline; use repeated runs and a merge step.

source: Li et al. (2024) ProgGen: Generating NER Datasets Step-by-step with Self-Reflexive LLMs
finding: Pipeline asks the LLM for attribute dimensions per domain, samples dimension-value pairs into prompts as diversity requirements, then self-corrects. Diversifying the entity side helped; diversifying sentence style tended to hurt.
numbers: Diversify-Y variants gave at least 2% F1 on average and up to 8% in nuanced domains versus a simple prompt; Diversify-X tended to lower F1; self-correction added 1-2% F1.
limits: Downstream NER data task, not ideation. Gains depend on which side is diversified.
agent_relevance: Attribute-box sampling can reduce quality if the varied dimension adds noise: choose dimensions that matter for the goal, and rank dimensions before enumeration.

source: Wang et al. (2025) DeepPersona: Scaling Deep Synthetic Personas
finding: Taxonomy-guided attribute sampling with a randomised walk and coverage priors beats naive LLM sampling for coverage; the authors state naive sampling saturates in diversity.
numbers: 32% higher attribute coverage and 44% greater profile uniqueness than baselines; personalised Q&A accuracy +11.6% across ten metrics; gap to real survey answers cut by 31.7%.
limits: Personas, not design concepts. Taxonomy mined from chat logs. Baselines chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: For gap 6: coverage priors favouring rare branches, stratified by similarity, is one tested sampling rule for a large attribute space. Not compared with random cells in a box.

source: Ackerman, Farchi, Katan, Raz (2024) Using Combinatorial Optimization to Design a High Quality LLM Solution
finding: Proposes covering arrays: choose a small set of factor-value combinations covering every pair (or triple) of values instead of the full product, on the argument that most effects come from low-order interactions.
numbers: No LLM accuracy numbers for the pruning rule; a simulated-data regression example shows factor effects can be estimated from the small set. Interaction order 2 or 3 typical.
limits: Method paper with simulated data; no head-to-head against random sampling on real LLM tasks.
agent_relevance: A principled answer to gap 6 for large boxes: code builds a pairwise covering array so every pair of values appears at least once, with far fewer cells than the product. Not validated for idea quality.

source: Ritchey (1998) Fritz Zwicky, Morphologie and Policy Analysis (quoting Zwicky 1966 and 1969)
finding: A second-hand check of Zwicky's claim. Zwicky called the method totality research that tries to derive all solutions; it may expose configurations overlooked by less structured methods. This is a design claim by the originator, not an experiment.
numbers: 75-cell 3-parameter box (5x3x5, Zwicky 1969 p.118); shelter example with 2304 configurations; a field of 50,000 configurations needs 450-550 pair evaluations; a 6-parameter shelter field over 100,000 configurations. No tested count of unconsidered configurations.
quote: which we might have overlooked by other -- less structured -- methods
limits: Advocate source; Zwicky 1969 itself not accessible. The 1947 vs 1962 dating of the 576 box remains unresolved.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 mostly closed: 'unconsidered configurations' is an assertion, not a measured result; do not cite it as evidence.

source: Chen, Tsang, Jing, Sun (2024) An LLMs-augmented Morphological Analysis Approach for Conceptual Design (DRS2024)
finding: Abstract page seen, PDF blocked (HTTP 403 / Cloudflare challenge). Three stages: decomposition, generation, combination, plus a feedback loop. Abstract claims better design quality, lower cognitive load and better designer-LLM interaction. A blog summary says three arms: manual morphological analysis, plain GPT-4, structured approach.
numbers: No sample size, scores or p-values retrieved.
limits: Numbers not obtained; the three-arm description is third-party.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open for Chen. The three-arm design (manual box, free GPT-4, structured box) is the right comparison for our own test.

source: Park and Geum (2025) LLM-enhanced idea generation: data-driven morphological analysis with LDA and NuNER, Computers and Industrial Engineering
finding: Only search-result snippets seen: matrix built from patent data with LDA topics and NuNER entities; LLM used on combinations; authors say a systematic matrix can be built from patents.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open for Park and Geum.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Terwiesch et al. (2024) Prompting Diverse Ideas: Increasing AI Idea Variance (via search summaries)
finding: Snippet only: prompt strategies including step-wise chain of thought, measured by cosine similarity. A Columbia write-up says chain of thought reduces fixation, personas help partition, and both together exceed humans.
numbers: Not opened this session; see b17 and c04 for numbers already read.
agent_relevance: No direct category-first versus combine-first test was found (gap 7); nearest are constraint and persona arms in d04.

source: Feng et al. (2025) Sage, human gold standard check (same paper as d03)
finding: Human judges are also inconsistent on pairwise preferences, so LLM-versus-expert agreement on compatibility is capped by expert noise.
numbers: Human evaluators on complex tasks: IPI 0.332 and TOV 6.523.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: measure expert repeat agreement first; do not expect LLM-expert agreement above it.

source: Search log for gaps 3, 5 and 7 (no direct source found)
finding: OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar rate-limited, arXiv API returned empty, last web search refused for budget. No study found that (a) measures LLM pair-compatibility judgments against experts in a morphological field, (b) independently measures how much cross-consistency assessment shrinks a real field and checks the survivors, or (c) compares category-first and combine-first for an LLM.
limits: Absence claim rests on about 8 searches plus the earlier agents; treat as not found, not as nonexistent.
agent_relevance: These gaps must be answered by our own test, not the literature.
